verdicts.reason: I reproduced it: a list<color> holding x112233 and a see-through x000000, 50 displays as {x112233, x000000, 50} while .size is 2. In an untyped list, {b, "a, b", 3} with b = x000000, 50 displays as {x000000, 50, "a, b", 3} with .size 3. verdicts.reason: I reproduced the main claim but not the crash. Adding a comment on its own line after a capsule's last self-call stops satl treating that call as a tail call. At 300,000 levels the plain version peaks at 18,664 KB (0.44 s). The comment version peaks at 1,107,296 KB (1.33 s), about 3.6 KB per level. A comment line followed by satellite.return() behaves the same (1,107,552 KB). An inline comment (down(n - 1) // c) and a blank line are both fine, at about 18.5 MB. At 3,000,000 levels I did NOT get the reported segfault: two runs with SATL_TIMEOUT=60 printed bottom/back and exited 0, peaking at 10.9 GB after 12.9 s and 21.7 s. The plain version stays near 19 MB at that depth. The hunter's 139 at 6.5 GB may depend on memory pressure. Either way, a comment turns constant-memory recursion into memory that grows with depth, which is two equivalent forms disagreeing plus runaway memory. The code comment at program_walk.cpp:423-431 records the author's ruling (2026-09-22) that a last-line self-call 'is a loop, not a deeper frame' and that 'LAST MEANS NOTHING OF THIS CAPSULE RUNS AFTER IT'. A comment runs nothing. The ruling that a middle self-call may crash does not cover this case. ERROR.md's accepted ~27,000 depth is about the C++ stack, and NEW_ERROR_LIST A8 is about middle recursion. Neither mentions comments, and none of the known lists or already-confirmed entries do either.

Re-ran all ~148 of the first hunter's programs in /tmp/claude-1000/-home-madness-code-satl/b70f905b-dca1-4f92-bbad-f66d8ce80b78/scratchpad/work/strings/ in bulk (results in strings-2/bulk/, one .out/.err/.time each). Its one apparent wrong answer (p23, a '}' "inserted" into a multi-line string) was a false alarm: the source itself had those '}' lines. My own minimal a1-a5 show that '{', '(' and '}' inside multi-line strings are kept exactly.

About 77 runs of my own in /tmp/claude-1000/-home-madness-code-satl/b70f905b-dca1-4f92-bbad-f66d8ce80b78/scratchpad/work/strings-2/.

Checked and found correct:
- All six escapes, byte-exact (\r kept). \x is refused.
- Curly quotes, single quotes, and an unclosed string are refused with clear messages.
- Literals up to 65,536 characters and 80,000 lines.
- An 8-million-character doubled string: find is correct.
- Unicode: .find counts characters. Comparisons follow the documented character table, and they agree with sort().by_name(), by_value(), .max and .min.
- upper/lower across about 40 scripts match Python, except the special cases that turn one letter into two (ß, ŉ, ﬀ, և), which ERRORS2 records as a choice. Other small differences, not reported: final sigma is not applied, and .reverse moves a combining mark or skin tone onto its neighbour (Python does the same).
- Empty-string edges and .find with an empty needle.
- .find counts from 0 and an absent text is refused with S420, both as the help says.
- .add, and - on strings (removes the first match).
- .bin and .hex, checked against Python for large values, with all their spellings. "+7" is refused.
- .number and its spellings.
- The number-first join rules (4 + "2" = 6, 4 + "abc" = 4abc).
- Joining 20,000 parts on one line, with + or with chained .add: 0.2 s.
- Strings holding // { } ( ) " and \\, and comments holding quotes and braces.
- Strings through capsules, as list items and as map keys.
- console.input with unicode and blank lines.

verdicts.reason: Reproduced exactly. For a plain string name, satellite.access wraps the raw text in quotes without escaping it. Then shown() turns control bytes into \xNN, a form satl itself refuses (S110). As a result, "a\n" and "a\\x0a" (== says false) are shown identically, and "x\", \"y" is shown as `"x", "y"`, which reads as two strings. For a list of strings, access (and console.display of a list) escapes correctly: {"x\", \"y"}. So the two forms disagree. Neither the known lists nor the salvage.json confirmed verifies mention access quoting or \x0a (searched titles and full entries). DESIGN.md has no ruling. The access help shows the value line in program form, e.g. {{"a": {1, 2}}, {"b": {3}}}.
verdicts.title: satellite.access shows a plain string's value unescaped, and a new line as \x0a (a form satl refuses), so different strings look identical

{

    satellite.variable.string two = "a\\x0a"
    satellite.access(one)
    satellite.access(two)
    satellite.console.display(one == two)
    satellite.return(satellite)
}

verdicts.expected: value  "a\n" for one and value  "a\\x0a" for two, escaped the way the value line already escapes a string inside a list ({"x\", \"y"}) and the way console.display of a list does.
verdicts.why_expected: The help for satellite.access (satellite.help/satellite.access/help_text.txt) shows values in program form, and the same command escapes a string inside a list correctly. Two strings that == calls different are shown the same, and the shown form \x0a is refused by satl's own checker (S110 '\x is not an escape satellite knows').
verdicts.variants: String q = "x\", \"y": access(q) shows `value  "x", "y"`, which looks like two strings. List m = {"x\", \"y"}: access(m) shows `{"x\", \"y"}` correctly. satellite.console.display(satellite.access(q)) (the string form) gives the same wrong text. With a tab or carriage return, the value shows as \x09 or \x0d. The original report also shows console.display({one, two}) printing {"say \"hi\"\n", "say \"hi\"\\x0a"} correctly.
verdicts.known_ref: none. It is not in ERROR.md, errors.md, ERRORS2.md, NEW_ERROR_LIST.md, CONTAINERS.md or the confirmed verifies in salvage.json. The hunter notes that the maps hunt reported something similar for map keys and values, but no such entry is among the confirmed verifies.
verdicts.source_location: /home/madness/code/cxx/satellite/satellite/bytecode/access_words.cpp:175 (as_text: returns "\"" + text + "\"" with the raw display_text of a string, with no escaping of \" \\ \n \t \r); access_words.cpp:212 (value_shown passes the whole thing through shown()); /home/madness/code/cxx/satellite/satellite/machine/shown.hpp:35 (turns bytes below 0x20 into \xNN)
verdicts.cause: For a top-level string, as_text puts the raw text of display_text between quotes and escapes nothing: embedded quotes and backslashes pass through unchanged. value_shown then runs shown(), the terminal-safety filter, which turns a newline, tab or CR into \x0a, \x09 or \x0d instead of the language's \n, \t, \r escapes. For list and map values, display_text already produces program-form literals with proper escapes, which is why only the plain-string path is wrong.

findings.title: Two threads writing the same field of one shared, unlocked object crash satl (double free / segfault) or get a false S999 OUT_OF_MEMORY. Affects string, list and big-number fields
findings.setup: spacesuit box has one protected field v and a capsule call_put() { v = v + "d" } (race_list: v.append(1) on a list<number>; race_bignum: v = v + 123456789012345678901234567890; race_number: v = v + 1). work(box b) calls b.call_put() 2000 times. main makes box b(), starts two threads on work(b) and joins both. There is no .lock(). The same crash came from the first hunter's p10_nolock, p11_unlocked_list, p11_unlocked_string, f4_unlocked_string and p12_unlocked_bignum in /tmp/claude-1000/-home-madness-code-satl/b70f905b-dca1-4f92-bbad-f66d8ce80b78/scratchpad/work/threads/ on the bulk re-run.
findings.observed: race_string, 3 of 3 runs: 'free(): double free detected in tcache 2' (twice) or 'free(): unaligned chunk detected in tcache 2', then 'timeout: the monitored command dumped core', exit 134, and no output. race_list, 3 of 3: 'double free or corruption (!prev)', exit 134. race_bignum, 3 runs: twice the full report 'S999: OUT_OF_MEMORY / the machine would not give satl the memory it asked for ... on a thread the program started', exit 48 (the program uses almost no memory), and once 'Segmentation fault', exit 139. The control race_number (small number field) prints 'done' with exit 0 in 3 of 3 runs. It only loses updates, as THREADS.md documents. Two threads writing DIFFERENT string fields of one object (distinct_fields.satl) are fine in 3 of 3 runs, and so is sharing that only reads (readonly_string.satl).
findings.expected: The program should finish and print 'done'. Without a lock the field's final value may be wrong (lost updates), but the interpreter must not abort, segfault or claim it is out of memory.
findings.why_expected: THREADS.md T2 gives the author's ruling that locks are off unless the user turns one on: 'Every object and every file has a lock, and it is off. Nothing is ever locked for it, and threads share it freely.' So lost updates are the program's to avoid. That is what the number field gives, and THREADS.md measures it (12,528 of 20,000). Nothing from the author rules that the INTERPRETER may crash on unlocked sharing. The only hedge is in the doc's own prose: the list-append row says 'not run: it can crash satl', and 'reading a list while another thread appends to it can crash satl'. Nothing says so for strings or big numbers, and the offered safety check is marked 'OFFERED, NOT ANSWERED'. A memory-safe language's interpreter aborting with glibc heap corruption, or reporting a false S999, counts as an error under the hunt's rules (crash 134/139, a refusal saying something false). Whether to rule it the program's fault is left to the author. As things stand it is unruled, and it is only half-documented, for lists alone.

findings.title: Every joined thread's answer is kept until the program ends: a loop that joins list answers grows without bound (1.5 GB against 44 MB for the same calls made directly)
findings.setup: build(n) returns a list of n numbers. main loops 200 rounds: satellite.variable.thread t = satellite.thread.new(build(50000)); t.start(); list<number> got = t.join(); total = total + got.size. It then displays total. The direct twin uses got = build(50000) instead. leak_reassign_100.satl declares t once outside the loop, with the same result.
findings.observed: Prints 10000000, exit 0, peak RSS 1,508,064 KB. 50 rounds: 398,480 KB. 100 rounds: 766,052 KB. It grows linearly, about 7.5 MB per round, which is exactly one 50,000-item answer. The direct twin: 44,208 KB at 200 rounds and 44,472 KB at 50. When the thread answers only l.size (leak_sizeonly_100.satl): 36,576 KB. So it is the joined answer that is never freed, not the thread's working memory. The first hunter's p84_answer_leak.satl (the one that 'timed out') is this program: 14.5 s and 1.5 GB, against 14.8 s and 45 MB for p84b_direct.satl. The time is the same either way. The memory is the thread-specific fault.
findings.expected: Memory flat, like the direct form: each round's answer is freed when 'got' and 't' are replaced.
findings.why_expected: The two forms are equivalent (THREADS.md: join() 'answers what f handed back') and should cost the same memory. Holding every answer for a possible second join (S724) should not outlive the thread variable. A loop of 200 ordinary joins reaching 1.5 GB is runaway memory for ordinary work. At DESIGN.md §13's target of many threads it would exhaust the machine.

findings.title: Threads that finish but are never joined keep about 17 KB each until the end: a fire-and-forget loop of 30,000 trivial threads reaches 520 MB
findings.setup: note(n) returns n. main loops i = 1..30000: satellite.variable.thread t = satellite.thread.new(note(i)); t.start(), with no join. It then displays 'all 30000 started'.
findings.observed: 'all 30000 started', exit 0, 1.41 s, peak RSS 520,048 KB. 5,000 threads: 101,856 KB. That is linear, about 16.8 KB for each finished, unjoined thread. The same count of threads, each joined (p83_20000.satl: 20,000 sequential start/join): 26,876 KB.
findings.expected: A thread that has finished and whose variable was replaced should be reclaimed, so memory stays about flat as in the joined case.
findings.why_expected: THREADS.md allows threads that are never joined ('Every thread still running is asked to stop and is waited for' at the end), so fire-and-forget is an ordinary pattern. DESIGN.md §13 targets 1,000,000 threads and measures 34.3 KB per LIVE thread. Here finished threads keep about half that forever, so a long-running program that starts threads without joining grows without bound. This is related to the joined-answer leak above: thread records are never freed.

verdicts.reason: Reproduced byte for byte. "ok".foreground(x00FF00).upper() displays ESC[38;2;0;255;0MOK ESC[39M into a pipe: the SGR final 'm' became 'M', display no longer recognises the code as a colour, and it writes the escape raw. .reverse() writes the codes backwards (m93[ESC kom0;552;0;2;83[ESC). .lower() and .upper().lower() come out plain 'ok', because the codes are already lower case. The help says the colour is part of the string and that display writes it plain into a pipe, and that .upper() gives the text in capitals and .reverse() turns the string round by character. Neither says the terminal codes are text to be changed. At a terminal, CSI ... M is Delete Line. None of the known lists or DESIGN.md mentions colour with case or reverse.
verdicts.title: .upper() and .reverse() on a coloured string rewrite its terminal codes, so raw escape bytes reach a pipe (ESC[38;2;0;255;0MOK), and at a terminal ESC[...M is 'delete lines'

'.upper() ... answers the text in capital letters'. '.reverse() turns a string round by character'. The coloured g on its own, and g.lower(), both display plain 'ok', so display strips codes that are intact.

"Ok".background(xFF0000).lower() gives ok. verdicts.reason: Reproduced. 5,000 unjoined threads peak at 102,064 KB, 30,000 at 519,604 KB and 60,000 at 1,021,620 KB, about 17 KB per thread and linear. The same 30,000-thread loop with t.join() peaks at 30,440 KB. The threads really have finished and their OS threads have exited. In a variant, a 3,000,000-step busy loop runs after 20,000 unjoined starts, and display(t) then says '(thread note, finished)'. Sampled during that loop, /proc shows Threads: 1025 (1,024 start-up threads plus main) while VmRSS stays at 355,184 kB. RSS drops to 49,240 kB only at satellite.return, when close_every_thread joins them all. It is not by design. THREADS.md allows threads that are never joined ('Every thread still running is asked to stop and is waited for' at the end). 'A thread that fails and is never joined still fails the run with its code' needs only the code kept, not the OS thread's stack. DESIGN.md §13 counts 34.3 KB per LIVE thread and says nothing about keeping finished ones. None of ERROR.md, errors.md, ERRORS2.md, NEW_ERROR_LIST.md or CONTAINERS.md mentions thread memory. The only thread-memory entry in salvage.json is about address space taken by the 1,024 start-up threads (bad_alloc under ulimit -v), which is a different cause. No confirmed-new title there matches.
verdicts.title: Threads that finish but are never joined keep about 17 KB of resident memory each until satellite.return: 30,000 fire-and-forget threads hold 520 MB, 60,000 hold 1 GB

verdicts.expected: Memory stays about flat, as in the joined case (30,000 start+join: 30,440 KB). A thread that has finished, and whose variable has been replaced, should give back its OS thread's stack. At most a few bytes (its code, for the 'fails and never joined still fails the run' rule) should be kept until the end.
verdicts.why_expected: THREADS.md makes never-joined threads an ordinary pattern: at the end every thread 'is asked to stop and is waited for'. DESIGN.md §13 prices a LIVE thread at 34.3 KB and aims for 1,000,000 threads. Here a thread that has ended still costs about half that for the rest of the run, so a long-running program that starts threads without joining grows without bound. Sampled live, satl had 1,025 OS threads (all 20,000 program threads had exited) yet held 355 MB until satellite.return.
verdicts.variants: 5,000 unjoined: 102,064 KB. 30,000: 519,604 KB. 60,000: 1,021,620 KB (linear, about 17 KB each). 30,000 joined: 30,440 KB. The variant with one t reassigned in the loop and a busy loop afterwards shows display(t) = '(thread note, finished)', live VmRSS 355,184 kB with Threads: 1025 during the busy loop, then 49,240 kB once the end-of-run close has joined them. Not tested here (sysctl cannot be changed): every unjoined thread also keeps its 128 MB stack mapping (kStackFloorBytes) plus a guard page. On a machine with the stock vm.max_map_count of 65,530 (this one has 1,048,576), about 32,000 finished-but-unjoined threads would probably exhaust mappings, and start() would then fail with S725.
verdicts.known_ref: none
verdicts.source_location: /home/madness/code/cxx/satellite/satellite/bytecode/thread_calls.cpp:149-158 (start: push_back into running().threads, then pthread_create joinable with a 128 MB stack); :106-120 (reap, the only pthread_join); :351-379 (close_every_thread, the only place running().threads is emptied); /home/madness/code/cxx/satellite/satellite/machine/stack_share.hpp:44 (kStackFloorBytes = 128 MB)
verdicts.cause: start() adds every thread's handle to the global running().threads list and creates a joinable pthread. Nothing removes a thread from that list, or joins or detaches its pthread, when the thread ends. Only the program's own join() (through reap) or close_every_thread at satellite.return does. glibc cannot free or reuse the stack of an exited joinable thread until pthread_join, so each finished, unjoined thread keeps its touched stack pages and thread control block resident (about 17 KB), plus a 128 MB stack mapping. One possible fix: when a thread ends, have it drop itself from the list and detach itself if no join has claimed it yet (os_joined under the lock). Keep only its code, so the 'fails and never joined still fails the run' rule still works.

findings.program: rep/p2_first_typed.satl vs rep/p2_first_untyped.satl; rep/p3_typed_local_copy.satl vs rep/p3_untyped_local_copy.satl; rep/p1_bsearch_typed_20000.satl (= the first hunter's tmp_scale.satl) vs rep/p1_bsearch_untyped_20000.satl
findings.setup: p2: `satellite.capsule first_of(satellite.container.list<satellite.variable.number> a) { satellite.return(a[1]) }`. main appends 1..20000 to a list<number> xs, then calls first_of(xs) 20,000 times and sums the answers. The untyped twin only changes the parameter to satellite.container.list. p3: the loop body is `satellite.container.list<satellite.variable.number> view = xs` then total = total + view[1]. p1: an ordinary binary search capsule with a list<number> parameter, 20,000 searches over 20,000 evens.
findings.observed: p2 typed: 20000, exit 0, real 14.9 s. p2 untyped: 20000, real 0.165 s. p3 typed local copy: real 15.0 s. p3 untyped: 0.20 s. p1 binary search typed: 10000, real 16.1 s (the first hunter saw 19.5 s, and at 20 s it timed out). p1 untyped: 0.9 s. Python bisect does the same work in 0.02 s. The first hunter's earlier numbers: 10,000x10,000 = 5.1 s typed vs 0.5 s untyped, and a recursive sum passing a typed list 10,000 deep = 4.3 s. The time grows with list size times call count.
findings.expected: Handing an already-typed list<number> to a list<number> parameter, or declaring a list<number> from one, should cost about the same as the untyped form, well under a second here.
findings.why_expected: satellite.help/satellite.container.list/help_text.txt: 'b = a COPIES the list ... and the copy costs nothing until one of them is written to'. Here the copy costs a full walk of 20,000 items every time, though every item was already checked when it went in (the help says a typed list checks 'on every way in'). Binary search, recursive list walks and helper capsules taking list<number> are ordinary, and they become quadratic. Verdict on tmp_scale.satl: it does not hang. It is this per-call re-check, and it finishes in 16 to 19.5 s.

findings.title: Two sibling blocks cannot declare the same name: if/else each with `string msg`, or two for loops each with `number sq`, are refused S202 'declared twice ... the second would quietly replace the first', though the first block has ended and for-loop counters can be reused
findings.setup: if(n > 2) { satellite.variable.string msg = "big"; display(msg) } else { satellite.variable.string msg = "small"; display(msg) }. f09: two sequential for loops over i, each body declaring satellite.variable.number sq. The for counter i is redeclared in the second loop without complaint.
findings.observed: S202: NAME_DECLARED_TWICE / satl(check): in satellite.main, msg is declared twice in the same capsule / directory: rep/d1_if_else_same_name.satl:13 / syntax: satellite.variable.string msg = "small" / this name is already declared where this line stands -- ... One name, one declaration -- the second would quietly replace the first. / machine code 26 name_declared_twice [exit 26]. f09: the same for sq at line 12 [exit 26].
findings.expected: Both run: big (d1), and 1 4 9 1 8 27 (f09). In C, C++, Java and 003-style braces each block has its own msg or sq.
findings.why_expected: Only one of the two declarations ever runs in d1, so nothing is 'quietly replaced'. A loop body that redeclares sq on every pass is accepted, and so is a for counter reused in a second loop (MILESTONES M20.A), so the rule treats blocks and for counters differently. This is the other side of ERRORS3.md #4 (block scope, his to rule), which covers only the leak. Report it with that ruling.

result.coverage: Re-ran all 116 of the first hunter's programs (realistic-programs/*.satl, min/, multi/) through the safe runner with my own HOME, as copies under realistic-programs-2/old (results in realistic-programs-2/bulk/*.out): 71 exit 0, the rest were deliberate probes. I checked every output line of the realistic exit-0 programs against python3 (Decimal where floats are involved) or the help: fizzbuzz, sieve to 10,000, float scores and grade letters, temperature table, bubble and insertion sort, word count map, bank spacesuit, matrix multiply, fib (recursive and list memo), binary search, gcd/lcm, collatz, to-do list, "item " + i + ": " + price, inventory map of lists, histogram, recursive nested-list tree sum, merge and quick sort, Pascal's triangle, tic-tac-toe, permutations, compound interest and loan payment, letter counts, a gradebook with a map of float lists, the p45 and p49 random big-number and float batteries. All were correct. I also wrote and ran 20 new realistic programs in realistic-programs-2/new, all correct: a student spacesuit with float lists, median and spread; matrix transpose, 4x4 determinant and fib(90) by matrix power; Josephus; a priority to-do insertion-sorted over a list of maps, with insert and remove_at; word-frequency map with remove_first/remove_last and literal duplicate keys; collatz with a 30,000-item list memo; mutual recursion 100,001 deep, hanoi(16) and ackermann(3,3); bank transfers with objects in maps and interest; a warehouse spacesuit with map<string, list> and map<string, float> fields; sieve to 1e6 (correct, 5.3 s); string ordering by sort, max/min and a hand loop, which agree. Judged by design, not reported: -x ^ 2 = 4 (consistent with the literal -2 ^ 2); 1.0/3*3 shows 1.0 but == 1.0 is false (the help says 32 places are shown and 128 kept); -7.5 % 2 = -1.5 and -17 / 5 = -3 (the help says C semantics); n++ as a statement is refused, the same family as n += 1; object == object refused, display(object) S210; 0 <= i < 10 refused clearly; && refused at run time, as the help says; a parameter named like a field or a variable named like a capsule gives S202 (one name, one declaration). Already known and not re-reported: a whole number in a float container; [n] after a call or method answer; names[1].size naming the list; S420/S501 paragraphs on lists. tmp_scale.satl does not hang: it is finding 4, the typed-list re-check, and completes in 16 to 19.5 s. About 50 satl runs of my own beyond the bulk re-run.

verdicts.cause: The comment token is a marker (0x0803, the text is not kept), and the rest of its line counts as the line's end. The else look-back (`while (back > 0 && code_at(row, back-1) == token::line_end_token) --back;`) and brace_after (`while (... code_at(row, at) == token::line_end_token) ++at;`) step over line ends but not over comment tokens. So a comment in between lands them on the comment token and not on the } or {. A trailing comment after if(...)/while(...) works only because past_the_statement runs on to the line end first. groups.title: Without .lock(), two threads writing one shared object field (string, list, big number) or appending to one file take no hold at all: glibc heap corruption (134), segfault (139) or a false S999, and the appended file is left empty
groups.merge_note: One cause: an object or file lock that is off takes nothing (object_lock.hpp; ObjectHold at expression.cpp:534), so two threads change heap-owning state at the same time. One fix: a memory-safety hold that is always on, separate from the author's lock.

groups.title: A bare block ({} or { ... }) ends the enclosing body at its }: the rest of main (satellite.return included) is skipped with exit 0, and inside a while the loop never advances (hang)

A statement that starts with a code that cannot start one (a sign, a literal, !, /*, )) is stepped over one code at a time and accepted: a continuation line starting with - or + is silently dropped (100 / - 30 holds 100), -n = 9 runs as n = 9, and a /* ... */ block runs its contents
groups.merge_note: All four come from the check_statement fallback at program_check.cpp:2242-2249 ("ONE CODE, NOT THE LINE ... ++at; return success") and its twin in run_statements. One fix: refuse (or join) a statement whose first code cannot start one.

groups.title: A capsule or library value named with one spelling of a method word is folded to that word's first spelling: two capsules color/colour in one spacesuit reach only one of them, m.as_number() runs number(), library values contain/contains collide, and library.upper reads a value written as up
groups.merge_note: One cause: the lexer turns every spelling of a method word into one method code, and token::method_name_of(code) gives back only the first spelling. The written name is lost before the capsule lookup (capsule_calls.cpp, suit_reach.cpp CapsuleTable::member) and the library lookup (library_values.cpp segment_at). One fix: keep the written spelling. #4 was already marked a duplicate of #2.

groups.title: A spacesuit capsule named lock() or unlock() never runs: the built-in object lock silently takes its place, and the declaration is not refused
groups.merge_note: Single finding. The cause differs from the spelling folding: lock_token is handled before capsules.member is consulted.

groups.title: Lines appended through one file handle stay in its 64 KiB buffer when a second handle or satellite.info reads the path: the reader sees too few lines, and the second handle's writes land before the held lines, out of program order

.upper() and .reverse() on a coloured string rewrite its embedded terminal codes, so raw escape bytes reach a pipe (ESC[38;2;0;255;0M), and at a terminal ESC[...M deletes lines

satellite.info.file, satellite.info.directory and satellite.directory.list resolve a relative path against the working directory, while satellite.file.* resolve it against the program's folder, so info can describe a different file from the one that was opened
List item matching (.contains, .index_of, .remove, list == list, index == index) never matches values of different kinds that == calls equal: a[3] == 3.0 is true, but a.contains(3.0) is false

A touching operator (n+1, 4+3, n**3, a*2) is refused only when its line runs: it is accepted silently in a branch not taken or a capsule never called, and refused after earlier lines have printed
groups.merge_note: The same finding reported twice: only refuse_if_reserved in the evaluator refuses tight_* tokens, and the checker never looks for them.

groups.title: s.reverse("x"), "abc".reverse(1, 2, 3) and n.reverse(99) are accepted silently with the argument ignored, while s.upper(1) is refused before anything runs
groups.merge_note: Kept separate from number-string-conversion#4. Both get past the checker's early "reverse -> success" line, but here the walker also ignores the brackets, and the fix is an argument-count check in both places.

groups.title: On a colour's declaring line, a colour variable whose name is spelled in hex letters and followed by a method (bead.transparency(20)) is refused as "read here as hex digits"
groups.merge_note: Single finding. color_check.cpp:80-94 does not test the_value_ends.

groups.title: A container type split after its < (list< newline number>) is not joined across lines: "a type was expected here"

A file whose name looks like a hex or binary literal (x1, xa, b1) cannot be included: include(x1) "names no file", include("x1") then gives "no capsule named area", and include(./x1) looks for ./.satl
groups.merge_note: The lexer fact is the same as in the hex-shaped-name group, but this is a different consumer (include_at accepts only name_token) with a different fix (a file name has no literal ambiguity), so it is kept separate.

groups.title: An else after a } that does not close an if (a while's or for's body, or a second else) passes the checker and is refused only when reached, as a one-line message with no S-code or line
groups.merge_note: The same finding reported twice: the else look-back (program_check.cpp:1759-1770) accepts any right_brace_token.

groups.title: A map declared with a key type that can never be a key (list, map, float) is accepted, and satellite.access prints a fill line (m[key] = 1) that is always refused
List .max, .min and .sort().by_value() put bools in order and succeed, while < and > refuse two bools because "only == and != order those"
A statement that only computes a method's answer (a.sort().by_value(), a.reverse(), a.sum, n.add(1)) is accepted and does nothing, while a bare a or a + 1 is refused as doing nothing
groups.merge_note: Kept separate from the unrecognised-statement-start group because the cause is in a different function: a_call_to_its_end accepts any chain that reaches the line end.

groups.title: Building a string with s = s + ... in a loop is quadratic: every + copies the whole left side (40,000 passes take 9.8 s for 230 KB)

Each map removal is O(n) (take_entry_out renumbers every row of the hash, and .remove(key) scans the entries), so emptying a map is quadratic: 20,000 remove_last() take 3.5-4 s, against 0.2 s for a list
Passing a list<number> to a list<number> parameter or declaration re-checks every item each time: 20,000 calls with a 20,000-item list take 15+ s typed, against 0.19 s untyped

Every started thread stays in the process-wide registry until satellite.return: a joined thread keeps its answer (614 MB at 80 rounds, against 44 MB for direct calls), and a finished thread that was never joined keeps ~17 KB of stack (1 GB at 60,000)
groups.merge_note: Same cause: start() pushes every handle into running().threads (thread_calls.cpp:152), and only close_every_thread empties it or joins/detaches the pthread.

groups.title: A comment line after a capsule's last self-call stops it being a tail call: memory grows with depth (1.1 GB at 300,000 levels, 10.9 GB at 3,000,000; 18 MB without the comment)
groups.merge_note: Same pattern as the if/else comment group (a comment_token is not stepped over the way a line end is), but it is in find_the_last_statements, with its own fix and symptom, so it is kept separate.

groups.title: Numbered but unbuilt method words that have no method code (.abs .sqrt .floor .digits, .to_binary on a hex, .at .substring .split .trim .starts_with .ends_with .resolved) are refused as "not one of its methods -- only a spacesuit has capsules", "no capsule named X" or S201, not S210 NOT_BUILT_YET
groups.merge_note: One cause: these spellings are missing from the method table (token_codes.hpp method_code_of). They lex as names and reach the spacesuit-member fallback (program_check.cpp:1216-1234), which never consults words.tsv. One fix: look the word up there (or add the spellings).

groups.title: A name spelled like a hex or binary literal (x1, xa, xff, b0, b1, b10) cannot be declared or used as a parameter, and the refusal either quotes a naming rule the name meets ("not a name -- a name is made of a-z, A-Z, 0-9 and _") or says there is no name
groups.merge_note: The same finding reported four times: the lexer makes x1 a hex literal, and the declaration and parameter checks give kNameRule without noticing the literal (program_check.cpp:2066-2070).

groups.title: A capsule whose name is not a name (x1, xa, b1, 5) gets no refusal on its header: the capsule is dropped silently, and the first line of its body is refused as "outside every capsule" or "satellite.return(satellite) goes inside satellite.main"
groups.merge_note: Same cause: capsule_header returns 0 with no trouble sentence when the name slot holds a literal (capsule_scopes.cpp:159-174 and :537-541).

groups.title: An expression that stops early for any reason gets the fixed "& | << >> !! are undecided" (or "math sign spacing") sentence at run time: n = n -1, n = 5 6, if (n = 5), 5., 0x1F, 0b101, and 1.2.3 with its caret past the end of the line
groups.merge_note: One sentence (kNotReadToTheEnd, program_walk.cpp:79-81) is reused for every early stop. One fix: name what the evaluator stopped at, and have the checker refuse two values standing side by side.

groups.title: satellite.directory.list() in a program is refused at run time with "satellite has no list type built yet to hold them (MILESTONES M14)", though M14's list is built
satellite.console.display() with no value gets past the check and stops at run time as S210 NOT_BUILT_YET, while two values are refused before anything runs
groups.merge_note: Single finding. takes_one tests for "(" in a spelling that has none (program_check.cpp:1494-1496).

groups.title: A capsule called on an empty spacesuit field is refused with a false math-sign / undecided-operator reason, and the "holds no object yet" refusal is unreachable
Displaying or joining a list of objects whose spacesuit declares to_string() is refused because "an object has no to_string capsule"

The checker does not judge a member reached through a map item or a nested container item (m[k].x, m[k].secret(), a wrong argument count): a field read is S201 "undeclared variable", and a protected capsule or a wrong count is refused only after earlier lines ran. Through a list item, both are refused before anything runs
groups.merge_note: Same cause and one fix: the item-member check (program_check.cpp:1304-1316) is reached only through where.lists, which records only a one-level list<spacesuit>.

groups.title: [n] after a call's answer, a method's answer, a list literal or a bracketed expression is refused at run time with a false math-sign / "& | << >> !!" hint, though the same value in a variable can be indexed
A not-built method on a list item or on a method's answer (names[1].size, a.join(", ").size) is refused only at run time, and the refusal names the list (names.size), which is a built word
Reading one character, s[1], passes the checker and is refused only at run time as S301 TYPES_DO_NOT_MEET, though the string help says it is refused with S210 before anything runs
groups.merge_note: The same finding reported twice: no checker rule covers [ ] on a string (expression.cpp:798).

groups.title: find/add/to_string/to_number/to_binary/to_hexadecimal on a declared name pass the checker whatever the receiver type and argument count (p.find on a percentage, a.add on a list, s.add() on a string), and are refused only after earlier lines ran
groups.merge_note: One cause: the early "return success" for of_a_string_or_number in method_on_a_name (program_check.cpp:~647 in the container branch, and :751-752 for other types). lists#5 also lists smaller pass-throughs in the same function (.keys/.values on a list, .reverse(1), later chain segments), but its main case is this one.

groups.title: The S210 hint from so_far_whose knows only file and container methods: .width on a binary and .transparency on a non-colour say "so far no type has it" (hex and colour do have them), and x.lock() says "so far it is a file's" (objects have it too)
groups.merge_note: Same function and one fix: so_far_whose (file_calls.cpp:242-256) consults only the file and container tables. threads-2#7 also notes that a missing thread method is filed under S301.

groups.title: A misspelled satellite word gets "did you mean" only at the start of a statement: as a type inside <...> or as a parameter type it is "<prefix> is not a type", and in value position (satellite.bool.flase) it is an undeclared variable
groups.merge_note: Same cause: word_it_most_likely_meant is called only on the statement-start path (program_check.cpp ~2031-2081). read_type_shape and the value-position name check never call it.

groups.title: A percentage, binary or hex name given an expression is told "ERROR: expected <first number><suffix>", built from its first literal alone: p = 1/4 is "expected 1%", p = 2 * 25% is "expected 2%", and a binary given a sum is "expected b1"
groups.merge_note: The same flaw, with the same fix, in parallel checks (program_check.cpp:329-334 and :357-372, hexadecimal_values.cpp:107-112): the first number_token is judged without looking at what follows it.

groups.title: Digits touching letters (1_000, 1e5, 1e-10, 5abc, 00ff00) are refused as an undeclared name made of the trailing fragment (_000, e, ff00). When such a name is declared, they pass the checker and fail at run time
groups.merge_note: One cause: the lexer ends a number at a letter and starts a name there, and only the colour-assignment check joins the two back together (color_check.cpp:119-129). One fix: notice a name that touches a number literal.

groups.title: The ! operator works as bool negation, but the only help page that mentions it lists it as COMING and says "None of this reads today"
groups.merge_note: The same finding reported twice (satellite.help/binary_and_hexadecimal/help_text.txt against expression.cpp:1057).

groups.title: .bin/.hex on a declared float name pass the checker and are refused with S210 only after earlier lines ran, while f.add and a fraction's .bin/.hex are refused before anything runs
groups.merge_note: Single finding. float_method_check passes to_binary and to_hexadecimal.

groups.title: .reverse() on a float or a fraction is refused as "not built yet" but filed as S301 TYPES_DO_NOT_MEET (exit 27) rather than S210 (exit 14), and only when its line runs
groups.merge_note: Single finding. The note on reverse-arguments-ignored says why it is kept separate.

groups.title: A string + an infinity is refused with the generic "no scenario for that pair" and no .string hint, although infinity.string() joins and a colour gets the hint
When a number comes first and the text spells a number, a refused pair is described by the converted value: 50% + "5" is quoted as "50% + 5", and x1F + "2.5" is called "a hex and a float"
A list or map literal with a comma missing between two items is refused as "opened with { and never closed with }", though the line closes it
a[1] += 2 (a compound assignment to an indexed item) gets an unrelated S110 "not a method call" sentence instead of S210 "not built yet -- write a[1] = a[1] + ..."
groups.merge_note: Single finding. It shares a_call_to_its_end with lists#11 and spacesuits-and-library#11, but each needs its own fix.

groups.title: The typed constructor satellite.container.list<type>() (and index<k, v>()) is refused only at run time, after earlier lines ran, as "there is no value here to work with"
A typed-container refusal names the declared type without its <type> ("was declared satellite.container.list"), though a bare list holds anything
The list help defines .sum as "every item added with +", but .sum refuses any string item, although 1 + "2" is 3 and "a" + "b" is "ab"
a.truncate(-1) is refused with "items count from 1", though truncate takes a count and truncate(0) is valid
A file word's text argument converts a whole number (f.append(42)) but refuses a float, percentage, hex, binary or fraction as "takes text", while "" + 2.5 joins
f.path answers the absolute resolved path, not the path as written, contrary to SATELLITE_FILE_OPERATIONS.md
display of a file is S210 NOT_BUILT_YET with no reason, while a list holding the file gets S301 with "a file has two strings ... write the one you mean"
groups.merge_note: Single finding. display_text drops the code and reason that to_string returns.

groups.title: A .number refusal on an argument row names "that argument.number" instead of what was written (args.argument_1.number)
A trailing operator before ) (display(n +)) is told "this + has none" [space], and a touching-sign refusal inside display puts its caret at column 0
groups.merge_note: Single finding (the wording of refuse_if_reserved and its missing position). Kept separate from the run-time-only group.

groups.title: A refusal on ** names ^, a sign the line does not contain (0 ** -1 is "the ^ of 0 and -1")
A fraction name given a spaced slash is always told it is "whole-number division", even for 1.0 / 3, and after 2/4 it names a pair "4 / 2" that was never written
display of a spacesuit object is refused as S210 only when its line runs, after earlier lines have printed
counter.bump() on a spacesuit's own name says counter has no satellite.variable line declaring it
Writing a field through a container item (things[1].v = 5, m["a"].v = 5) gets an unrelated S110 "not a method call" sentence, while reading it, or writing a.v, gets S230
other.field inside the spacesuit's own capsule is refused because "fields are reached from inside the spacesuit only", though the line is already inside it
A map's .insert/.remove_at/.truncate refusal suggests age.keys.insert(...), a line that is itself refused (S110 "has no name to change")
Refusals about a name declared satellite.container.map call it an "index" ("the index is empty"), though the help says a refusal uses the word that was written

On a declared map, .append/.insert/.remove_at/.truncate/.index_of/.search pass the checker and are refused only after earlier lines ran, while .sum/.max/.min/.join/.reserve are refused before anything runs
groups.merge_note: Single finding. index_refuses never consults a_position_method, which is a different missing check from string-number-methods-skip-receiver-check.

groups.title: A multiple refusing a container whose items are the wrong kind says only "it holds a map/list, and this name takes ...", dropping the real reason
satellite.access position letters collide with the name shown: a list named m is shown as m[n][m], and a list named n as n[n]
satellite.return(satellite)} as main's last line is refused S103 at a line past the end of the file, which asks for the return that is already there
groups.merge_note: Single finding. Its cause differs from blank-line-before-main-brace-s103.

groups.title: The run-time S240 (an answer was used, but none was handed back) names the capsule's header line, not the call whose answer was used
"abc".replace("a", "b") on a string literal is refused (S210) only after earlier lines ran, while s.replace on a name, and .size/.contains on a literal, are refused before anything runs
display(t.join()) of a thread that handed nothing back is refused at run time as S210 NOT_BUILT_YET, while display(greet()) is S240 before anything runs
A thread joining itself is refused as S110 LINE_NOT_UNDERSTOOD, not S728 WAIT_NEVER_ENDS
S728 WAIT_NEVER_ENDS for a circle made only of joins explains it as "the object's lock it needs is held by a thread", though no lock is involved
